content:
Hi everyone, new contributor here :wave:

I'm working on formalizing the arithmetical hierarchy (in recursion theory) in Lean, and I'm thinking of opening PRs for Mathlib. I'd love early feedback before I start opening PRs. This is my first contribution, so I'm keen to get feedback on Mathlib conventions and style.

My code covers (the foundations of) the arithmetical hierarchy, but also oracle computation (extending Nat.Partrec.Code) and results on relativized computation. I have formalized, e.g., Kleene normal form theorems, infrastructure for showing completeness for the various levels of the hierarchy (and some example results), Rice's theorem, Shoenfield lemma, Turing jump. My plan is to submit all/most of this as several subsequent PRs, each reasonable in scope/size.

One concrete question that I have: I started building the arithmetical hierarchy on Nat as basis, and then have wrappers for general Primcodable types. It seems that for Mathlib, sometimes (or most of the time?) things are defined for Primcodable directly. Is there a preference for doing things differently from what I did?

Also: any advice for a first-time contributor on things to watch out for beyond the standard contribution guidelines would be very welcome.

My code is on GitHub: https://github.com/rdehaan/ArithmeticalHierarchy/.

Thanks a lot! :smile:
Did you use AI to generate this code? (Your repository has one huge commit with most of the code. This is different from e.g. how I would work by hand, which is one reason I'm asking.)

If so, be aware that AI-written code is quite far from mathlib's quality standards. (I don't know, but could imagine the situation being similar in cslib.) You should also be aware that reviewers may be reluctant to review AI-generated code: review is a lot of work, and as a reviewer you want to be really sure that a human reads, understands and learns from your comments. That's much easier to believe if they also authored the code by hand. You may find #use-of-ai (written for mathlib) helpful.

Michael Rothgang said:

If so, be aware that AI-written code is quite far from mathlib's quality standards. (I don't know, but could imagine the situation being similar in cslib.)

CSLib is younger and so has less experience with quality control, but our AI policy states that "CSLib in general follows the Mathlib policy on use of AI" and links to the same document as above.

I have considered CSLib, but I thought that Mathlib was more suitable topic-wise. (Recursion theory fits under mathematical logic, classically.) I'm open to contributing to CSLib instead if there's a preference for that.

The large 'initial commit' in the repository has a reason. This grew out of a private repo that I have where I'm developing recursion theory exercises / material for my teaching. I developed it gradually in that repo, but for the sake of clarity (and because I don't want my students to find all the exercise solutions) I moved it to a new (public) repo.

I read the #use-of-ai guideline. I have been using Aristotle in my learning process of Lean. For example, there were some lemmas where I didn't know yet how to prove them, and I asked Aristotle to help me close them. I don't intend to create PRs with low-quality code, so if you think the code needs quality improvement before a PR, please tell me. I'm very keen on learning, and want to only open PRs that are as little work to review as possible (I'm aware that the backlog of PRs is huge), that's why I'm asking here. :)

Michael Rothgang said:

Did you use AI to generate this code? (Your repository has one huge commit with most of the code. This is different from e.g. how I would work by hand, which is one reason I'm asking.)

I want to point out that this is not always a sign of AI code. I often work like this with manually written code.

I formulate and work privately on the side for the same reasons.. the one time I did not (due to many more technical moving parts) is the only time I have been summarily baited of my work... i.e. that random "gift" 3-4weeks ago that appeared out of the blue with massive changes and integrations.... the one that had no author ... ya... that was my Navier Stokes Clay Millennium Proof. Now deconstructed and handed to the lake piranhas lol...
Keep your stuff private yall.
